title: Beyond skin deep: physiologic oral pigmentation as an overlooked validation gap in AI-assisted oral cancer screening
desc: AI-assisted oral cancer screening tools, exemplified by MeMoSA, have been validated almost exclusively in Asian populations. We propose a testable hypothesis: physiologic oral pigmentation, which varies by race independent of pathology, may cause classifiers to misclassify normal variation as suspicious or miss camouflaged lesions. Following precedent from pulse oximetry and dermatology AI, we call for pigmentation-stratified validation before deployment in racially diverse settings such as the United States.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pulmonary Hypertension: Advancements, Opportunities, and Challenges.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a progressive cardiopulmonary disorder associated with high morbidity and mortality. Delayed diagnosis, heterogeneous disease phenotypes, and variable treatment responses remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a promising tool for improving PH management. AI-based models have demonstrated promising performance in screening, diagnosis, classification, risk stratification, and prognosis prediction using multimodal data such as electrocardiography, chest radiography, computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, echocardiography, and electronic health records. Furthermore, AI may support individualized risk assessment, treatment-response prediction, early identification of right ventricular deterioration, and longitudinal remote monitoring. Emerging technologies, including explainable AI, federated learning, large language models, and digital twins, may further advance precision medicine in PH. Despite these advances, data quality, interpretability, privacy, and clinical implementation of AI remain challenges. This review summarizes current applications, opportunities, and challenges of AI in PH and discusses future directions for AI-assisted precision healthcare.

Learning health system frameworks and the integration of artificial intelligence and data science in United States health care: a scoping review
desc: Learning Health Systems (LHSs) use routinely collected data to generate evidence that informs practice through continuous learning cycles. Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science may strengthen this model, but how LHS frameworks and AI applications relate remains unclear. We mapped LHS frameworks and their components and examined how AI and data science are integrated. Searches identified U.S.-based, English-language studies published January 2007–August 2025; two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, resolving disagreements by consensus. We included 54 framework studies (24 [44%] conceptual adaptations; 30 [56%] real-world implementations) and 30 AI/data science studies. Five components recurred across the frameworks: data infrastructure and interoperability, governance and stakeholder engagement, learning and improvement cycles, evidence generation and translation, and equity and ethics. Relative to framework studies, AI studies less often addressed governance and stakeholder engagement (17% vs 35%) or equity (13% vs 22%), emphasizing computational over organizational functions. Most AI studies (27/30) focused on the data-to-knowledge phase; only three extended to knowledge-to-practice, and none described practice-to-data feedback with post-deployment outcomes informing model updating. AI applications capture only part of the LHS vision, concentrating on knowledge generation with less attention to the organizational and feedback mechanisms needed to translate insights into practice and sustain learning.

title: Artificial intelligence for Traditional Chinese Medicine classic formula development: a technology readiness assessment using metabolic syndrome as a case study.
desc: [Frontiers in pharmacology] Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas, developed through millennia of clinical practice, represent a rich legacy of approximately 100,000 documented prescriptions (99,584 named formula entries in the second edition of the Dictionary of Traditional Chinese Medicine Formulas), yet on average fewer than ten new TCM products were approved annually by China's NMPA from 2013 to 2024 (77 approvals in total). The experience-based screening paradigm is misaligned with the precision medicine framework demanded by metabolic syndrome (MetS), a multi-target disorder affecting an estimated 1.54 billion adults (95% CrI 1.35-1.76) in 2023. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-encompassing knowledge graphs (KGs), large language models (LLMs), and high-throughput experimentation-has been proposed as a solution, its actual readiness for TCM development remains unclear. This review critically examines KG, LLM, and high-throughput validation technologies enabling precision phytomedicine for MetS, providing a realistic roadmap for AI-driven TCM research and development. The three technology streams exhibit asymmetric readiness. At the stream level, knowledge-graph approaches span Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3-6, large language model approaches span TRL 1-5, and high-throughput validation platforms span TRL 3-5. LLM development is limited by three TCM-specific hallucination types that lack evaluation benchmarks. KG entity recognition is the most mature component, yet reasoning is hindered by the absence of negative data, missing dose-time dimensions, and unencoded monarch-minister-assistant-envoy hierarchies. High-throughput platforms are technically feasible but remain mismatched to MetS functional endpoints-tumor-derived organoid paradigms show limited direct transferability and would require substantial adaptation. Precision phytomedicine must follow a "foundations before algorithms" sequence: institutionalize negative data, build TCM-Hallu benchmarks, establish functional-endpoint evaluation, and develop AI-assisted regulatory review. Algorithmic advances will remain in an incomplete information space until knowledge infrastructure gaps are closed.

Measurement fidelity and external validation of automated breast DCE-MRI segmentation
desc: Automated breast dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) segmentation could facilitate quantitative tumor measurement, but geometric overlap alone does not establish the fidelity of mask-derived measurements. We developed an enhancement-aware three-dimensional MedNeXt framework with gated skip fusion and boundary supervision and evaluated it in a retrospective multi-cohort design spanning locked internal testing, source-held-out assessment, retrospective external validation, and radiologist review. Measurement fidelity was the primary endpoint. Across 521 paired internal-test and DUKE cases, median errors were 9.7% for tumor volume, 1.8 mm for 3D maximum surface diameter, and 10.2% for operational enhancement-defined volume, with corresponding ICCs of 0.97, 0.80, and 0.97. Median Dice was 0.831 internally and 0.823 in the DUKE source-held-out stratum, and was 0.812 and 0.806 in the BC-MRI-SEG and public BreastDCEDL_AMBL retrospective external-validation cohorts, respectively, using the frozen checkpoint without external-label tuning. No major correction was required for 78 of 80 masks in the blinded two-reader review. In 276 paired response-analysis cases, AUROC was 0.732 with automatic geometry and 0.757 with expert geometry (difference, −0.025; 95% CI, −0.095 to 0.045); discrimination non-inferiority was not demonstrated. These findings support automated segmentation as a starting point for radiologist-supervised retrospective quantitative research within the evaluated cohorts, while distinguishing measurement fidelity from downstream predictive equivalence.

title: Generative AI, Health Misinformation, and Medical Deepfakes: Implications for Diagnostic Safety and Clinical Practice-A Narrative Review.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce persuasive health information in the form of text, synthetic images, cloned voices and deepfake videos. It can also be used to create fictitious professional identities. This narrative review describes how synthetic claims, fabricated evidence and simulated identities are used to disguise misleading health information and give it the appearance of authenticity especially with regard to diagnostic safety and clinical practice. Literature identified through Web of Science and Scopus was synthesized across text image audio video and multimodal formats; current evidence indicates that generative AI can produce highly credible but inaccurate health content. Source authority, message framing and professional identity cues influence trust and verification behavior, while disease-specific evaluations show that high average accuracy may coexist with clinically important omissions, missed referrals, hallucinated findings and poor calibration. In medical imaging, errors may arise both from incorrect interpretation and from manipulation of the diagnostic evidence itself. Detection, evidence-based verification, provenance, literacy interventions, and governance provide complementary safeguards, although real-world and longitudinal evidence remains limited. Clinical evaluation should therefore consider task-specific performance, source authenticity, human oversight, and the consequences of individual errors alongside overall accuracy.

Imaging as a Surgical Decision System in Modern Gynecologic Oncology.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Imaging traditionally supports gynecologic oncology through diagnosis, staging, and estimation of resectability. Contemporary treatment, however, requires longitudinal decisions about which lesion matters, when local intervention is justified, and which modality is proportionate. This critical narrative review proposes imaging as a longitudinal surgical decision system integrating disease trajectory, treatment response, target selection, operative planning, and post-intervention assessment. We define imaging-target mismatch as discordance between the radiologically dominant lesion and the lesion with greatest clinical actionability, and operationalize the disease-modifying surgical window as open, uncertain, or closed across six decision domains. Serial imaging may reveal response-created opportunities, oligopersistence, oligoprogression, competing dissemination, or the need for tissue confirmation, while CT, MRI, ultrasound, and FDG PET/CT provide complementary decision-specific information. Three-dimensional reconstruction, intraoperative imaging, radiomics, and artificial intelligence may enhance planning, but require prospective external validation and should support rather than replace multidisciplinary judgment. Decision-oriented reporting should communicate the target, lesion-level trajectory, competing disease, anatomical feasibility, residual uncertainty, and the relevance of findings to the proposed intervention. Imaging should therefore guide not only what can be treated, but what should be treated, when, and for what therapeutic purpose.

An Interpretable Multimodal Deep Learning Framework Integrating MRI and Clinical Data via Bidirectional Cross-Modal Attention for Improved Cardiac Disease Detection.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] Cardiovascular diseases continue to be the primary cause of mortality worldwide; however, precise diagnosis is often limited by dependence on individual data modalities and the unclear nature of traditional deep learning models. In this study, we introduce an explainable multimodal deep learning framework that simultaneously analyzes cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and structured clinical variables through a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism that operates on token sequences. The architecture utilizes modality-specific encoders ResNet-50 for imaging and a multilayer perceptron for clinical data interconnected through attention that dynamically aligns complementary information, reducing feature dilution and modal dominance. A multitask objective that includes classification, contrastive alignment (InfoNCE), and regularization further reinforces semantic consistency across modalities. Integrated post hoc explainability modules, such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping for spatial localization and SHapley Additive exPlanations for clinical feature attribution, offer transparent decision support. Tested on a cohort of 12,847 patients using fivefold cross-validation, the framework achieved an accuracy of 94.2% and an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.97, significantly surpassing unimodal and traditional multimodal baselines (p < 0.01). The explanations generated showed 91% concordance with independent cardiologist evaluations. The findings presented herein were derived through internal five-fold cross-validation conducted at a solitary tertiary care institution, thereby substantiating internal validity while limiting multicenter generalizability; consequently, external validation is requisite for broader applicability. These results demonstrate that attention-driven multimodal fusion, combined with post hoc explainability, provides both strong diagnostic performance and clinically useful transparency, positioning the framework as a promising internally validated approach and a foundation for future external validation.

Global Trends of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Family Medicine: A Comprehensive Scopus-Based Bibliometric Analysis (2016-2026).
desc: [Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)] Aim: To map recent artificial intelligence research in family medicine and primary care against an earlier 2015-2024 bibliometric baseline. Methods: Scopus was searched on 9 July 2026 for 2016-2026 publications. One researcher screened 3452 articles and reviews; 132 topical and 13 language exclusions left 3307 records. Manual title, DOI, and Scopus-identifier checks identified no duplicates. VOSviewer 1.6.21 and Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.4.1; R 4.6.1) supported descriptive analysis and mapping. Results: Output increased from 531 in 2024 to 792 in 2025 (49.2%). The 2025 and partial 2026 component contained 1407 records (42.5%); 615 were dated 2026. The USA led publication and raw citation rankings (711 publications; 18,671 citations), while China preceded the United Kingdom in publication count. The Journal of Medical Internet Research (78 publications) and Scientific Reports (69) led the venues; seven top ten venues were shared with the earlier study. Language model terminology coexisted with later-positioned explainability, risk stratification, and diagnostic accuracy terms. Conclusions: This updated map quantifies post-2024 activity and identifies continuity and corpus-dependent differences in geography, dissemination, and evaluation-related vocabulary. Single-database and English language coverage, single-researcher screening, unadjusted citations, and incomplete 2026 coverage limit inference. The findings describe research activity, not clinical adoption, safety, effectiveness, or causality.

title: Beyond Mucosal Healing: Quantitative Transmural Phenotyping to Assess Therapeutic Response and Support Precision Treatment in Crohn's Disease-A Narrative Review.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Crohn's disease (CD) is a transmural disorder in which mucosal healing may coexist with persistent mural, mesenteric, or penetrating disease. Cross-sectional imaging can therefore extend assessment beyond lesion detection toward quantitative transmural phenotyping, using imaging-derived markers to characterize inflammatory activity, structural and fibrotic burden, extramural involvement, and longitudinal treatment response. This narrative review synthesizes recent evidence on intestinal ultrasound (IUS), including contrast-enhanced ultrasound and elastography, magnetic resonance enterography (MRE), computed tomography enterography (CTE), multienergy CT, radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI). IUS and MRE currently provide the most clinically mature approaches for serial assessment through bowel wall thickness, vascularity, composite activity indices, and measures of transmural response or healing. Conventional CTE remains important for structural and penetrating complications but is primarily morphologic and semi-quantitative. Multienergy CT introduces material-specific biomarkers, particularly iodine-based measures of inflammatory activity, whereas radiomics and AI remain largely investigational. Across modalities, persistent imaging abnormalities after treatment may provide prognostic information beyond mucosal assessment, but definitions, acquisition protocols, thresholds, and validation strategies remain heterogeneous. Quantitative transmural phenotyping may complement clinical, biochemical, endoscopic, and histological assessment, but standardization, multicenter validation, and prospective imaging-guided trials are required before routine precision-management implementation.

Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020-2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.

title: Challenges of Single-Reference Benchmarks for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model-Based Decision Support.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] This viewpoint addresses developers and evaluators of large language model (LLM)-based clinical decision support systems. Although recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate multiple clinical reasoning domains, many still rely substantially on reference decision agreement-whether model outputs conform to predefined decisions. Our aim is to clarify when such agreement remains useful, when it becomes insufficient for complex or preference-sensitive decisions, and how it can be complemented by reasoning-centered assessment. Clinical decision-making often depends on structured reasoning under uncertainty, integrating probabilistic evidence, contextual constraints, and patient values. Using oncology as an illustrative domain, we argue that some decision variability is a structural feature of clinical reasoning rather than noise or error. Used alone in such settings, single-reference benchmarks may conflate reasonable divergence with incorrectness and reward answer imitation over transparent reasoning. We conclude that reference decision agreement should be retained for tasks with stable ground truth but supplemented by evidence grounding, reasoning quality, patient-centeredness, and safety checks for open-ended clinical decision support. This multidimensional approach is intended to support safer and more clinically meaningful evaluation.

title: Converging Paths: Artificial Intelligence for Integrating Biological and Digital Biomarkers in Personalized Longevity Medicine.
source: PubMed · International journal of molecular sciences
desc: [International journal of molecular sciences] Ageing is a multidimensional biological process characterised by interacting molecular, physiological, functional, and environmental changes that chronological age alone cannot adequately represent. The rapid development of epigenetic clocks, proteomic and metabolomic signatures, imaging-derived biomarkers, wearable sensors, and digital phenotypes has created an increasingly rich but fragmented landscape of aging biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential integrative framework that can combine these heterogeneous data streams and convert them into multidimensional estimates of biological age, health risk, functional reserve, and potentially treatment response. Recent studies demonstrate that molecular and clinical information can be integrated into composite aging measures, while independent work shows that wearable movement data, retinal imaging, and speech characteristics can provide non-invasive digital representations of aging-related phenotypes. The emerging concept of multimodal aging clocks extends these approaches by integrating physiological, clinical, imaging, and molecular measurements into a common representation of biological aging.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Australian Public-Funded Dental Services.
desc: [Australian dental journal] A proportion of Australians encounter substantial unmet oral health needs despite eligibility for government-subsidised care. Yet, government dental services operate within a fragmented, mixed public-private system with limited capacity to support priority populations. The National Oral Health Plan (2015-2024) responds to this visible and measured need for priority. As the next National Oral Health Plan is developed, these priorities provide a timely basis to consider whether emerging technologies can support access and system performance without reproducing existing inequities. This narrative review aims to examine the potential uses, evidence for, challenges and implementation considerations of the use of Artificial Intelligence including machine learning, in Australian public-funded dental services, and to examine the implications for access, equity, governance, community co-design and workforce capability. The evidence is interpreted through a multidimensional framework for access to care, while retaining the National Oral Health Plan (2015-2024) as the policy context. Limited research conducted in Australian-based healthcare settings shows evidence for public dental system-level improvements for triage, risk stratification, service planning and workflow, but also identifies material concerns about opportunity cost, human oversight, non-representative data, algorithmic bias, cultural safety, Indigenous Data Sovereignty and clinician education. Artificial Intelligence and machine learning technologies may support more responsive public-funded dental services, but technical performance alone is not evidence of improved access or equitable care. Intentional, values-led implementation requires representative data, Indigenous-led governance, community co-design, transparent evaluation, human accountability and a digitally capable workforce.

title: Classification Performance of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Common Skin Lesions in the Emergency Department: A Multicenter Preliminary Validation Study.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Background/Objectives: Initial classification of skin lesions in the emergency department (ED) is difficult when dermatology consultations are limited. This study externally validated a deep learning (DL) algorithm for classifying three common ED skin lesions and explored whether algorithmic pre-classification was associated with changes in the classification performance of medical staff. Methods: A ResNet-50-based algorithm was developed using 6000 clinical images from 4815 patients. For external validation, 100 images from an independent institution were classified by the algorithm and nine medical staff members (three emergency medicine specialists, three residents, and three physician assistant [PA] nurses). Fifteen days later, the staff reclassified the same randomly reordered images with the algorithmic pre-classification provided. Results: In external validation, the algorithm showed an overall accuracy of 0.96 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-0.99), lesion-specific balanced accuracies of 0.95-0.96, and a macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.95-1.00). Unassisted, the three PA nurses differed significantly from the algorithm for urticaria and herpes zoster (all p < 0.01, McNemar's exact test). After receiving algorithmic assistance, all medical staff showed a balanced accuracy of 0.97 or higher for all three lesions. In the mixed-effects model, assistance was associated with higher odds of correct classification (odds ratio 25.9, 95% CI 11.7-57.2), and inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ) increased from 0.70 to 0.97. Conclusions: The algorithm demonstrated high classification performance on independent external validation, and algorithmic assistance was associated with improved classification performance, with the largest absolute gains among medical staff with lower unassisted accuracy. As these findings are exploratory, they should be confirmed in randomized prospective studies.

title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for ICU pharmacotherapy training: Supporting learning while preserving clinical judgment.
desc: [Journal of critical care] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in critical care practice at a time when pharmacotherapeutic decisions are becoming more complex, data-intensive, and time-sensitive. For medical residents and fellows, this creates both educational opportunities and challenges, as AI may support learning but must not replace the development of independent clinical judgment. This perspective examines potential applications of AI in ICU pharmacotherapy training, including support for just-in-time learning, case-based practice, and bedside decision support. Key limitations and risks, such as misinformation, cognitive offloading, deskilling, privacy and data security, and bias in model outputs, are discussed along with possible mitigation strategies. Future training should prioritize building competencies related to AI-assisted clinical decision-making, including critical appraisal of AI-generated outputs and communication of AI-informed decisions within interprofessional teams. AI-supported pharmacotherapy training should be guided by clear boundaries around use and continued emphasis on building foundational pharmacotherapy knowledge, patient-specific reasoning, and clinical judgment.

title: MRI-derived synthetic [¹⁸F]FET PET in neuro-oncology: evaluation in glioma grading and differentiation from solitary brain metastasis.
desc: [Neuroradiology] O-(2-[18F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine positron emission tomography ([18F]FET PET) is clinically useful in neuro-oncology but limited by cost and availability. We assessed the clinical utility of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived synthetic [18F]FET PET. A total of 489 patients with histologically confirmed gliomas or brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. A deep learning model generated synthetic PET images from multimodal MRI in the overall cohort and subgroups. Synthetic PET was evaluated against reference PET for image similarity by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) analysis by Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis, and blinded reader assessment for glioma grading and high-grade glioma (HGG) versus solitary brain metastasis (SBM) differentiation using receiver operating characteristic analysis with area under the curve (AUC). Synthetic PET showed high similarity to reference PET in the overall, glioma, and metastasis groups (PSNR, 34.7-35.5 dB; SSIM, 0.90-0.96), and SUVR correlations were strong (r = 0.77-0.93, all P 0.05). MRI-derived synthetic [18F]FET PET may enhance glioma grading and HGG-SBM differentiation, providing a PET-like alternative when FET PET is unavailable.

title: Toward Clinically Trustworthy Deep Learning in Cardiology: A Unified Mathematical Synthesis of Representation, Optimization, and Reliability.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized cardiovascular medicine by allowing for automated analysis of electrocardiography, imaging of the heart, and multimodal clinical datasets. Although there have been impressive advancements in terms of predictive performance, the deployment of DL methods in a clinical setting remains limited due to lack of sufficient mathematical understanding around the concepts of uncertainty, robustness, fairness, explainability, and generalizability. Methods: In this work, a systematic review is conducted using PRISMA principles on 79 peer-reviewed articles published from 2017 until 2025, with a unifying mathematical perspective on the notion of trustworthy deep learning in cardiology. Results: We find that there is significant discrepancy between prediction accuracy and clinical reliability, with little emphasis placed on mathematical guarantees, reproducibility of evaluation procedures, calibration, or robustness verification. To address this challenge, we propose a conceptual mathematical framework which brings together the elements of representation learning, optimization, and trustworthiness into a unified audit of AI in cardiac care. We note that the presented indices are purely theoretical and are meant to provide guidance for future standardization, and as such do not represent actual clinical metrics. Conclusions: Although our paper does not propose any new predictive algorithms, we do contribute a strong theoretical basis for the evaluation and development of clinically reliable deep learning algorithms in cardiology.

title: From Anatomy to Pathology: How Well Can AI Interpret Static Point-of-Care Ultrasound Images?
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence may support point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) interpretation in emergency medicine, but its performance on static images and sensitivity to acquisition context remain uncertain. This study evaluated GPT-5.6 Sol and assessed whether probe-region information improves interpretation across view/plane, anatomy, and pathology domains. Methods: In this paired comparative in silico study, 92 educational ultrasound images from seven anatomical regions were assessed under standardized uninformed (image only) and informed (image plus probe-region code) prompting conditions. Two independent raters scored responses against textbook-based references in three domains: view/plane identification, anatomical structure identification, and pathological finding detection. Each domain was scored from 0 to 2. Disagreements were resolved by a third ultrasound expert, and fully correct responses were defined as domain scores of 2. The primary outcome was the total performance score (0-6). Secondary outcomes included domain-specific scores, fully correct response rates, and exploratory subgroup analyses. Wilcoxon signed-rank and McNemar tests assessed paired scores and fully correct rates, respectively. Results: Total performance was higher with informed prompting (median (interquartile range), 5 (4-6) versus 4 (2-5); p < 0.001). Interrater agreement was substantial to almost perfect across evaluation domains (quadratic-weighted κ = 0.750-1.000). Fully correct rates increased from 58.7% to 88.0% for view/plane identification and from 47.8% to 82.6% for anatomical structure identification (both p < 0.001). Pathological finding detection improved from 35.9% to 48.9% (p = 0.002). Among pathology-positive images, missed or incorrectly labeled pathology remained frequent (44.8%) despite informed prompting. Regional differences in total performance were significant only under uninformed prompting (p = 0.002). Conclusions: Probe-region information substantially improved view/plane and anatomical structure identification, but pathological finding detection remained comparatively weak. In static POCUS interpretation, improved anatomical recognition did not translate into reliable pathology detection. Persistent false-negative and false-positive errors do not support independent diagnostic use. Potential applications in POCUS education and anatomical labeling require further validation.

title: Workflow Design, Editor Expertise and case Typology for AI-Generated OSCE Scripts.
desc: [Medical science educator] The pilot comparability study by Josan and colleagues comparing GPT-4-generated and expert-written OSCE standardized patient scripts offers timely insights for medical education. This letter highlights three considerations. First, the "AI-only" arm was not human-free but reflected an expert-supervised iterative loop, suggesting that the key contrast lies in workflow design rather than authorship. Second, the AI+human scripts scored highest in clinical accuracy yet lowest in realism, consistent with evidence that combined human-AI workflows can underperform the stronger party alone, particularly when humans act as final arbiters rather than co-producers. Third, large language models may be better suited to knowledge-intensive, protocol-driven OSCE cases than to communication-heavy scenarios. Future studies should distinguish subject-matter from task-specific editor expertise and develop a case typology to guide appropriate AI deployment.

title: Calibration-Aware Heterogeneous Multimodal Ensemble for Multi-Class Skin Lesion Diagnosis.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Background: Reliable classification of skin lesions is essential for early melanoma detection; however, substantial visual overlap among lesion types and pronounced class imbalance continue to limit the performance and reliability of existing automated systems. These challenges motivate the integration of complementary visual representations with clinical metadata to improve discrimination across lesion classes. Methods: This study introduces a calibrated multimodal ensemble learning framework for skin lesion classification. The proposed framework combines visual features extracted from Swin Transformer, EVA-02, and CoAtNet architectures with patient age and anatomical region information. A two-stage adaptive temperature scaling is applied to calibrate the predicted probabilities of the ensemble. Results: Experimental evaluation on the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC 2019) dataset demonstrates strong classification performance, achieving a macro-F1 score of 0.91 and a macro-AUC of 0.99. The framework further showed robust generalization on the official ISIC 2019 benchmark set, attaining a balanced accuracy of 0.65. The external validation on the PH2 dataset yielded a macro-F1 score of 0.93 and an ROC-AUC of 0.96. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that combining heterogeneous visual representations, clinical metadata, and calibration-aware ensemble learning provides a robust and trustworthy solution for skin lesion classification and computer-aided dermatological diagnosis.

title: Multimodal Large Language Model Discrimination of Poster-to-Manuscript Conversion at the 2022-2023 Society of Surgical Oncology Annual Meetings.
desc: [Annals of surgical oncology] Whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can identify publishable scientific work is untested. This study evaluated whether GPT-4.1 mini could distinguish Society of Surgical Oncology (SSO) posters that reached full-text publication using poster content alone and examined characteristics associated with conversion. This study retrospectively analyzed 597 posters from the 2022-2023 SSO Annual Meetings. Each poster was scored by GPT-4.1 on five research-quality domains during 30 runs at temperature zero. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Multivariable logistic regression tested whether the score added information beyond poster and investigator characteristics. Of 597 posters, 295 (49.4%) reached full-text publication. The composite score showed modest discrimination (AUC, 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57-0.66), with no evidence that performance differed across categories (interaction P = 0.90). Each 5-point increase in score was associated with higher adjusted odds of publication (odds ratio [OR], 1.45; 95% CI, 1.21-1.75), and adding the score to poster characteristics improved discrimination (ΔAUC, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.01-0.08). Design rigor, data quality, conclusion validity, and publication potential scores were associated with publication, but novelty was not. Multicenter status, first-author training status, and author sex were not significantly associated with publication. Lower adjusted odds for Hispanic first authors did not persist after multiplicity correction (OR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.15-0.81). The GPT-4.1 mini scores modestly distinguished posters that reached publication and added information beyond poster characteristics. Multimodal large language models merit further study as instruments for examining and strengthening scholarly work rather than as arbiters of publishability.

title: Physics-Consistent Sparse Learning for Cross-Domain Rotor Fault Diagnosis.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Robust rotor fault diagnosis is challenging when labeled fault data are limited and operating conditions differ between synthetic and real environments. Existing domain-adaptation methods can reduce distributional discrepancies, but they may retain redundant features and provide limited physical interpretability. This study proposes a physics-guided sparse-entropy domain adaptation framework for robust rotor fault diagnosis under such distribution shifts. Bearing eccentricity and damping are identified from experimental measurements and used to construct a physics-consistent rotor model. Synthetic fault data are then generated by incorporating representative defects, including unbalance and misalignment, while unlabeled signals, acquired from a laboratory rotor test rig, are used as the target domain. A ResNet-based feature extractor is trained using a hybrid strategy that combines labeled synthetic data with unlabeled experimental data. Maximum Mean Discrepancy and a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network are employed to reduce the source-target distribution discrepancy. In addition, sparsity and entropy regularization are incorporated into the objective function to suppress redundant representations and enhance fault-discriminative features. A Monte Carlo simulation-based optimization strategy is used to balance classification, domain alignment, and sparse-entropy constraints. Experimental results demonstrate an average target-domain accuracy of 94.04%, with a transfer gap of only 5.16%. The proposed framework also achieves higher diagnostic accuracy than DANN, Correlation Alignment, and MMD-based approaches. These results demonstrate its potential for data-efficient and physically interpretable rotor condition monitoring under varying operating conditions.

title: 2D Memory Transistors for Neuromorphic Computing.
desc: [Materials (Basel, Switzerland)] The boom in artificial intelligence has driven in-memory computing for high speed and power efficiency. Motivated by the need, neuromorphic computing (NC)-mimicking biological spike neural networks-ies a promising alternative that requires artificial neurons and synapses to construct NC circuits. 2D memory transistors have received intensive interest in recent research for NC applications as both artificial neurons and synapses with additional advantages for high device density and energy efficiency. This review intends to highlight recent progress made in the exploration of 2D memory transistors and their implementation into electrical and optoelectronic NC circuits. Discussions of remaining challenges and future perspectives are also provided.

title: Evaluating SegFormer and U-Net for Real-Time Sensor-Based Sorting: From Semantic Segmentation to Sorting.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Conventional sensor-based sorting systems often rely on handcrafted image-processing features, which are highly task-specific, require expert knowledge, and are difficult to transfer to new sorting tasks. In contrast, deep learning enables automated feature learning and has previously been shown to outperform color-based sorting in several application scenarios. In this study, we investigate the suitability of two deep-learning-based semantic segmentation architectures, U-Net and SegFormer, for real-time sensor-based sorting. Their performance is evaluated in both offline experiments and practical sorting trials for the applications bulky waste sorting and hibiscus tea sorting. Both models proved suitable for the investigated tasks. U-Net showed slight advantages in inference speed and purity, reaching purities of 95.9 wt.% for bulky waste and 100.0 wt.% for hibiscus tea. SegFormer achieved almost equal results for sorting hibiscus tea and four percentage points lower purity for sorting bulky waste. Real-time applicability was demonstrated for SegFormer variants B0 to B3, which met the required throughput of 62 megapixels per second. Overall, the results show that transformer-based models are a viable and promising alternative to CNNs for real-time sensor-based sorting.

title: A Variational Autoencoder Network for Heartbeat Signal Reconstruction and Breathing-State Classification Using 24 GHz Radar Sensors.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Wireless radar sensors can remotely detect vital signs. This study investigates the wireless monitoring of physiological signals induced by respiration and heartbeat to classify breathing states. Two 24 GHz radar sensors are used. Noise, harmonics, and intermodulation products affect the measured physiological signals and can make heartbeat identification and analysis challenging. Deep-learning techniques have recently been used to denoise and classify signals in wireless communications. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) have also been used for signal and image processing. Multilayer VAEs support sequential learning by optimizing generative-model parameters and reducing reconstruction error. This study investigates the separation of measured heartbeat and respiratory signals and the reduction in noise and the effects of limited random body movements using VAEs under controlled conditions. Two radars are positioned in front of and behind a human subject to record vital signals simultaneously. The separated and denoised heartbeat signals are input to a ResNet network to classify normal and fast breathing states. The proposed method achieves 99.7% accuracy on the reported experimental dataset.
